On cabled knots, Dehn surgery, and left-orderable fundamental groupsThanks: Both authors partially supported by NSERC postdoctoral fellowships

Adam Clay Address:  CIRGET, Université du Québec à Montréal, Case postale 8888, Succursale centre-ville, Montréal QC, H3C 3P8. Email address: aclay@cirget.ca and Liam Watson Address: Department of Mathematics, UCLA, 520 Portola Plaza, Los Angeles CA, 90095. Email address: lwatson@math.ucla.edu
Date: March 11, 2011
Abstract.

Previous work of the authors establishes a criterion on the fundamental group of a knot complement that determines when Dehn surgery on the knot will have a fundamental group that is not left-orderable [6]. We provide a refinement of this criterion by introducing the notion of a decayed knot; it is shown that Dehn surgery on decayed knots produces surgery manifolds that have non-left-orderable fundamental group for all sufficiently positive surgeries. As an application, we prove that sufficiently positive cables of decayed knots are always decayed knots. These results mirror properties of L-space surgeries in the context of Heegaard Floer homology.

Definition 1.

A group GG is left-orderable if there exists a partition of the group elements

G=𝒫⊔{1}⊔𝒫−1G=\mathcal{P}\sqcup\{1\}\sqcup\mathcal{P}^{-1}

satisfying 𝒫⋅𝒫⊆𝒫\mathcal{P}\cdot\mathcal{P}\subseteq\mathcal{P} and 𝒫≠∅\mathcal{P}\neq\emptyset. The subset 𝒫\mathcal{P} is called a positive cone.

This is equivalent to GG admitting a left-invariant strict total ordering. For background on left-orderable groups relevant to this paper see [2, 6]; a standard reference for the theory of left-orderable groups is [12]. As established by Boyer, Rolfsen and Wiest [2] (compare [11]), the fundamental group π1​(K)\pi_{1}(K) of the complement of a knot KK in S3S^{3} is always left-orderable. Indeed, this follows from the fact that any compact, connected, irreducible, orientable 33-manifold with positive first Betti number has left-orderable fundamental group [2, Theorem 1.1]. However, the question of left-orderability for fundamental groups of rational homology 33-spheres is considerably more subtle (see [2, 6]) and seems closely tied to certain codimension one structures on the 33-manifold (see [2, 3, 17]). Continuing along the lines of [6] this paper focuses on Dehn surgery, an operation on knots that produces rational homology 33-spheres. We recall this construction in order to fix notation and conventions.

For any knot KK in S3S^{3} there is a preferred generating set for the peripheral subgroup ℤ⊕ℤ⊂π1​(K)\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}\subset\pi_{1}(K) provided by the knot meridian μ\mu and the Seifert longitude λ\lambda. The latter is uniquely determined (up to orientation) by the existence of a Seifert surface for KK. We orient μ\mu so that it links positively with KK, and orient λ\lambda so that μ⋅λ=1\mu\cdot\lambda=1. For any rational number rr with reduced form pq\frac{p}{q} we denote the peripheral element μp​λq\mu^{p}\lambda^{q} by αr\alpha_{r}. At the level of the fundamental group, the result of Dehn surgery along αr\alpha_{r} is summarized by the short exact sequence

1→⟨⟨αr⟩⟩→π1​(K)→π1​(Sr3​(K))→1.1\to\langle\langle\alpha_{r}\rangle\rangle\to\pi_{1}(K)\to\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(K))\to 1.

Here ⟨⟨αr⟩⟩\langle\langle\alpha_{r}\rangle\rangle denotes the normal closure of αr\alpha_{r}, and Sr3​(K)S^{3}_{r}(K) is the 33-manifold obtained by attaching a solid torus to the boundary of S3∖ν⁡(K)S^{3}\smallsetminus\nu(K), sending the meridian of the torus to a simple closed curve representing the class

[αr]∈H1​(∂(S3∖ν⁡(K)),ℤ)/{±1}.[\alpha_{r}]\in H_{1}(\partial(S^{3}\smallsetminus\nu(K));\mathbb{Z})/\{\pm 1\}.

We will blur the distinction between αr\alpha_{r} as an element of the fundamental group or as a primitive class in the (projective) first homology of the boundary, and refer to these peripheral elements as slopes.

While many examples of rational homology 3-spheres have left-orderable fundamental group [2], there exist infinite families of knots for which sufficiently positive Dehn surgery (that is, along a slope parametrized by a suitable large rational number) yields a manifold with non-left-orderable fundamental group [6]. To make this precise, consider the set of slopes

𝒮r={αr′|r′≥r}\mathcal{S}_{r}=\{\alpha_{r^{\prime}}|r^{\prime}\geq r\}

for some fixed rational rr.

Definition 2.

A nontrivial knot KK in S3S^{3} is called rr-decayed if, for any positive cone 𝒫\mathcal{P} in π1​(K)\pi_{1}(K), either 𝒫∩𝒮r=𝒮r\mathcal{P}\cap\mathcal{S}_{r}=\mathcal{S}_{r} or 𝒫∩𝒮r=∅\mathcal{P}\cap\mathcal{S}_{r}=\emptyset.

The existence of decayed knots is established in [6]. For example, the torus knot Tp,qT_{p,q} is (p​q−1)(pq-1)-decayed (for p,q>0p,q>0), and the (−2,3,q)(-2,3,q)-pretzel knot is (10+q)(10+q)-decayed for odd q≥5q\geq 5 (see Theorem 11). Our interest in this property stems from the following:

Theorem 3.

If KK is rr-decayed then π1​(Sr′3​(K))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}(K)) is not left-orderable for all r′≥rr^{\prime}\geq r.

As a result, it is not restrictive to assume that rr is a positive rational number since π1​(S03​(K))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{0}(K)) is always left-orderable [2]. Notice however that it is not immediately clear how Theorem 3 might be applied in practice, as there is no obvious method for checking when a knot is rr-decayed. For this reason, in Section 1 we describe an equivalent formulation of rr-decay whose statement is more technical, but easier to verify, than the definition. Together with the proof of Theorem 3, the results of Section 1 provide a useful refinement of the ideas from [6].

Results connecting left-orderability and Dehn surgery may be expected to mirror similar results relating to L-spaces, since there is no known example of an L-space with left-orderable fundamental group, while many L-spaces have fundamental group that is not left-orderable. (see [1, 5, 6, 16, 21]). Recall that an L-space is a rational homology sphere with Heegaard Floer homology that is as simple as possible, in the sense that rk⁡HF^​(Y)=|H1​(Y,ℤ)|\operatorname{rk}\widehat{\operatorname{HF}}(Y)=|H_{1}(Y;\mathbb{Z})| (see [15]). Theorem 3 mirrors a fundamental property of knots admitting L-space surgeries: if Sn3​(K)S_{n}^{3}(K) is an L-space, then Sr3​(K)S^{3}_{r}(K) is an L-space as well for any r≥nr\geq n.

In the interest of further investigating left-orderability of fundamental groups of 3-manifolds along the lines of [6], we consider the behaviour of Dehn surgery on cables of rr-decayed knots (for necessary background, see Section 2). Denoting the (p,q)(p,q)-cable of the knot KK as Cp,q​(K)C_{p,q}(K), the main theorem of this article is:

Theorem 4.

If K is rr-decayed then Cp,q​(K)C_{p,q}(K) is p​qpq-decayed whenever qp>r\frac{q}{p}>r.

The proof of Theorem 4 is contained in Section 2. Notice that combining Theorem 11 and Theorem 4 provides a rather large class of knots for which sufficiently positive surgery yields a non-left-orderable fundamental group.

Dehn surgery on cabled knots and non-left-orderability of the resulting fundamental groups may again be viewed in the context of Heegaard Floer homology. Referring to knots admitting L-space surgeries as L-space knots, Hedden proves:

Theorem 5.

[9, Theorem 1.10] If KK is an L-space knot then Cp,q​(K)C_{p,q}(K) is an L-space knot whenever qp≥2​g​(K)−1\frac{q}{p}\geq 2g(K)-1.

Here, the quantity g⁡(K)g(K) is the Seifert genus of KK. Note that the converse of this statement has been recently established by Hom [10].

In order to assess the strength of Theorem 4, it is natural to ask when Dehn surgery on a cable knot yields a manifold that has left-orderable fundamental group. It turns out that, in the case that KK is rr-decayed, Theorem 4 is close to describing all possible non-left-orderable surgeries on a cable knot Cp,q​(K)C_{p,q}(K), in the following sense:

Theorem 6.

Suppose that CC is the (p,q)(p,q)-cable of some knot. If r∈ℚr\in\mathbb{Q} satisfies r<p​q−p−qr<pq-p-q, then π1​(Sr3​(C))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(C)) is left-orderable.

This result is a special case of a more general observation pertaining to satellite knots that is discussed in Section 3. Notice that Theorem 6 makes no reference to the original knot being rr-decayed. However, restricted to rr-decayed knots, Theorem 4 and Theorem 6 combine to produce an interval of surgery coefficients for which the left-orderability of the associated quotient is not determined. More precisely:

Question 7.

If KK is rr-decayed and CC is a (p,q)(p,q)-cable of KK with qp>r\frac{q}{p}>r, can Theorem 4 and Theorem 6 be sharpened to determine when π1​(Sr′3​(C))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}(C)) is left-orderable for r′r^{\prime} satisfying p​q−p−q<r′≤p​qpq-p-q<r^{\prime}\leq pq?

1. A practical reformulation of Theorem 3

We begin with a reformulation of rr-decay that will be essential in connecting this work with the results of [6]. This will require the following lemma:

Lemma 8.

Let GG be a left-orderable group containing elements g,hg,h. If g∈𝒫g\in\mathcal{P} implies h∈𝒫h\in\mathcal{P} for every positive cone 𝒫\mathcal{P}, then g∈𝒫g\in\mathcal{P} if and only if h∈𝒫h\in\mathcal{P}.

Proof.

We need only show the converse, namely h∈𝒫h\in\mathcal{P} implies g∈𝒫g\in\mathcal{P} for every positive cone 𝒫⊂G\mathcal{P}\subset G. For a contradiction, suppose this is not the case, so there exists a positive cone such that h∈𝒫h\in\mathcal{P} and g∉𝒫g\notin\mathcal{P}. Consider the positive cone 𝒬=𝒫−1\mathcal{Q}=\mathcal{P}^{-1}, defining the reverse ordering of GG. This gives g∈𝒬g\in\mathcal{Q} and h∉𝒬h\notin\mathcal{Q}, contradicting our assumption. ∎

Proposition 9.

A knot KK is rr-decayed if and only if for every positive cone 𝒫⊂π1​(K)\mathcal{P}\subset\pi_{1}(K) there exists a strictly increasing sequence of positive rational numbers {ri}\{r_{i}\} with ri→∞r_{i}\to\infty satisfying

  • (1)

    r=r0r=r_{0}, and

  • (2)

    αr∈𝒫\alpha_{r}\in\mathcal{P} implies αri∈𝒫\alpha_{r_{i}}\in\mathcal{P} for all ii.

Proof.

Suppose that KK is rr-decayed , and let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be any positive cone. Choose a strictly increasing sequence of rational numbers {ri}\{r_{i}\} with r0=rr_{0}=r and ri→∞r_{i}\to\infty. Whenever αr=αr0∈𝒫\alpha_{r}=\alpha_{r_{0}}\in\mathcal{P} we have 𝒮r∩𝒫≠∅\mathcal{S}_{r}\cap\mathcal{P}\neq\emptyset, so that 𝒮r∩𝒫=𝒮r\mathcal{S}_{r}\cap\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{S}_{r} since KK is rr-decayed. It follows that αri∈𝒮r⊂𝒫\alpha_{r_{i}}\in\mathcal{S}_{r}\subset\mathcal{P} for all ii.

To prove the converse, let 𝒫\mathcal{P} be a positive cone for π1​(K)\pi_{1}(K). Fix a strictly increasing sequence {ri}\{r_{i}\} of rational numbers limiting to infinity and satisfying (1) and (2). Suppose that αr∈𝒫\alpha_{r}\in\mathcal{P}, then by assumption αri∈𝒫\alpha_{r_{i}}\in\mathcal{P} for all i>0i>0.

Now suppose that μm​λn\mu^{m}\lambda^{n} is an element of 𝒮r\mathcal{S}_{r}. Choose ri,ri+1r_{i},r_{i+1} with corresponding reduced forms piqi,pi+1qi+1\frac{p_{i}}{q_{i}},\frac{p_{i+1}}{q_{i+1}} such that ri<mn<ri+1r_{i}<\frac{m}{n}<r_{i+1}. By solving

qi​a+qi+1​b\displaystyle q_{i}a+q_{i+1}b =c​n\displaystyle=cn
pi​a+pi+1​b\displaystyle p_{i}a+p_{i+1}b =c​m\displaystyle=cm

we can find positive integers a,ba,b and cc such that (μpi​λqi)a​(μpi+1​λqi+1)b=(μm​λn)c(\mu^{p_{i}}\lambda^{q_{i}})^{a}(\mu^{p_{i+1}}\lambda^{q_{i+1}})^{b}=(\mu^{m}\lambda^{n})^{c}. Explicitly, Cramer’s rule gives

a=|nqi+1mpi+1|,b=|qinpim|,c=|qiqi+1pipi+1|;a=\left|\begin{matrix}n&q_{i+1}\\ m&p_{i+1}\end{matrix}\right|,\quad b=\left|\begin{matrix}q_{i}&n\\ p_{i}&m\end{matrix}\right|,\quad c=\left|\begin{matrix}q_{i}&q_{i+1}\\ p_{i}&p_{i+1}\end{matrix}\right|;

note that all these quantities are positive because of our restriction ri<mn<ri+1r_{i}<\frac{m}{n}<r_{i+1} (compare [6, Lemma 17]) . This shows that μm​λn\mu^{m}\lambda^{n} is positive, since its cc-th power is expressed as a product of positive elements. Hence 𝒮r∩𝒫=𝒮r\mathcal{S}_{r}\cap\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{S}_{r}.

This establishes the implication αr∈𝒫⇒𝒮r⊂𝒫\alpha_{r}\in\mathcal{P}\Rightarrow\mathcal{S}_{r}\subset\mathcal{P} for every positive cone 𝒫\mathcal{P}. By Lemma 8, this is equivalent to 𝒮r∩𝒫=𝒮r\mathcal{S}_{r}\cap\mathcal{P}=\mathcal{S}_{r} or 𝒮r∩𝒫=∅\mathcal{S}_{r}\cap\mathcal{P}=\emptyset for every positive cone 𝒫\mathcal{P}, so that KK is rr-decayed. ∎

Remark 10.

In practice, it is often more natural to establish αr∈𝒫\alpha_{r}\in\mathcal{P} implies αriwi∈𝒫\alpha_{r_{i}}^{w_{i}}\in\mathcal{P} for all ii, where wi∈ℕw_{i}\in\mathbb{N} (see in particular the proofs of Lemma 13 and Lemma 14). This situation arises when one constructs (for a given positive cone 𝒫\mathcal{P}) a sequence of unreduced rationals {ri}={piqi}\{r_{i}\}=\{\frac{p_{i}}{q_{i}}\} for which gcd⁡(pi,qi)=wi≥1\gcd(p_{i},q_{i})=w_{i}\geq 1, and μp0​λq0∈𝒫\mu^{p_{0}}\lambda^{q_{0}}\in\mathcal{P} implies μpi​λqi∈𝒫\mu^{p_{i}}\lambda^{q_{i}}\in\mathcal{P} for all ii. Notice that the implication αr∈𝒫\alpha_{r}\in\mathcal{P} implies αriwi∈𝒫\alpha_{r_{i}}^{w_{i}}\in\mathcal{P} still allows us to apply Proposition 9, since αriwi∈𝒫\alpha_{r_{i}}^{w_{i}}\in\mathcal{P} if and only if αri∈𝒫\alpha_{r_{i}}\in\mathcal{P} (this simple observation holds in any left-orderable group). Ultimately, this results in more flexibility in selecting the sequence {ri}\{r_{i}\}.

The equivalence established in Proposition 9 shows that all examples considered in [6] are rr-decayed for certain rr, as [6, Corollary 11] is a special case of Proposition 9.

Theorem 11.

[6, Theorem 24, Theorem 28 and Theorem 30]

  1. (1)

    The (p,q)(p,q)-torus knot is (p​q−1)(pq-1)-decayed for all positive, relatively prime pairs of integers p,qp,q.

  2. (2)

    The (−2,3,q)(-2,3,q)-pretzel knot is (10+q)(10+q)-decayed for all odd q≥5q\geq 5.

  3. (3)

    The (3,q)(3,q)-torus knot with one positive full twist added along two strands is (3​q+2)(3q+2)-decayed, for all positive qq congruent to 22 modulo 33.

Proof.

We consider the case of KqK_{q}, the (−2,3,q)(-2,3,q)-pretzel knot with q≥5q\geq 5 odd, the other cases are similar. Set r=10+qr=10+q, and ri=r+ir_{i}=r+i. It is shown in [6] that for every positive cone 𝒫\mathcal{P} in π1​(Kq)\pi_{1}(K_{q}), the implication αr∈𝒫⇒αri∈𝒫\alpha_{r}\in\mathcal{P}\Rightarrow\alpha_{r_{i}}\in\mathcal{P} holds for all i≥0i\geq 0. This means that for every left-ordering of π1​(Kq)\pi_{1}(K_{q}), the integer sequence {ri}\{r_{i}\} satisfies the properties required by Proposition 9, and we conclude that KqK_{q} is rr-decayed. ∎

Note that the above proof illustrates some particularly special behaviour, as the rational sequences {ri}\{r_{i}\} required by Proposition 9 (which a priori may be different for each left-ordering) are replaced by a single integer sequence sufficient for every left-ordering. Thus, Proposition 9 provides a more workable method (than used previously) for checking when a knot has surgeries that yield a non-left-orderable fundamental group. Combined with the material established in [6, Section 2], we provide a short proof of Theorem 3.

Proof of Theorem 3.

For contradiction, assume that π1​(Sr′3​(K))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}(K)) is left-orderable for some r′≥rr^{\prime}\geq r, and consider the short exact sequence

1→⟨⟨αr′⟩⟩→iπ1​(K)→fπ1​(Sr′3​(K))→1,1\rightarrow\langle\langle\alpha_{r^{\prime}}\rangle\rangle\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i}}{{\rightarrow}}\pi_{1}(K)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle f}}{{\rightarrow}}\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}(K))\rightarrow 1,

as defined in the introduction. Let μ,λ∈π1​(K)\mu,\lambda\in\pi_{1}(K) denote the meridian and longitude. Since π1​(Sr′3​(K))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}(K)) is left-orderable, ⟨⟨αr′⟩⟩∩⟨μ,λ⟩=⟨αr′⟩\langle\langle\alpha_{r^{\prime}}\rangle\rangle\cap\langle\mu,\lambda\rangle=\langle\alpha_{r^{\prime}}\rangle (see proof of [6, Proposition 20]). In particular, if we fix an arbitrary rational number s0>r′s_{0}>r^{\prime}, then f⁡(αs0)≠1f(\alpha_{s_{0}})\neq 1. Thus, we may choose a positive cone 𝒬\mathcal{Q} in π1​(Sr′3​(K))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}(K)) that contains f⁡(αs0)f(\alpha_{s_{0}}). Next, choose a positive cone 𝒬′⊂⟨⟨αr′⟩⟩\mathcal{Q}^{\prime}\subset\langle\langle\alpha_{r^{\prime}}\rangle\rangle not containing αr′\alpha_{r^{\prime}}, and define a positive cone 𝒫⊂π1​(K)\mathcal{P}\subset\pi_{1}(K) by

𝒫=i⁡(𝒬′)⊔f−1​(𝒬).\mathcal{P}=i(\mathcal{Q}^{\prime})\sqcup f^{-1}(\mathcal{Q}).

Note that αr′∉𝒫\alpha_{r^{\prime}}\notin\mathcal{P}, and αs0∈𝒫\alpha_{s_{0}}\in\mathcal{P}.

This is a standard construction for creating a left-ordering of a group using a short exact sequence, here the result is a left-ordering of π1​(K)\pi_{1}(K) with positive cone 𝒫\mathcal{P}, relative to which the subgroup ⟨⟨αr′⟩⟩\langle\langle\alpha_{r^{\prime}}\rangle\rangle is convex. Because ⟨⟨αr′⟩⟩\langle\langle\alpha_{r^{\prime}}\rangle\rangle is convex, the intersection ⟨⟨αr′⟩⟩∩⟨μ,λ⟩=⟨αr′⟩\langle\langle\alpha_{r^{\prime}}\rangle\rangle\cap\langle\mu,\lambda\rangle=\langle\alpha_{r^{\prime}}\rangle is convex in the restriction ordering of ⟨μ,λ⟩\langle\mu,\lambda\rangle. Therefore, [6, Proposition 18] shows that all slopes αs\alpha_{s} with s>r′s>r^{\prime} must have the same sign. In particular, since αs0\alpha_{s_{0}} is positive it follows that all slopes αs\alpha_{s} with s>r′s>r^{\prime} are positive, so that

Q∩𝒮r={αs|s>r′}.Q\cap\mathcal{S}_{r}=\{\alpha_{s}|s>r^{\prime}\}.

Therefore, KK is not rr-decayed. ∎

We remark that there is a more geometric argument establishing Theorem 3, that relies upon an understanding of the topology of the space of left-orderings of ℤ⊕ℤ\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z} (see [18, Section 3] and [4, Chapter 6]). Roughly, every left-ordering of the knot group π1​(K)\pi_{1}(K) restricts to a left-ordering of the peripheral subgroup that defines a line in ℤ⊕ℤ\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}, with all positive elements of ℤ⊕ℤ\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z} on one side of the line, and all the negative elements on the other side. As a result, given two rationals r1<r2r_{1}<r_{2} corresponding to slopes αr1\alpha_{r_{1}} and αr2\alpha_{r_{2}} that have the same sign in every left-ordering, no left-ordering can restrict to an ordering of the peripheral subgroup with corresponding slope ss between r1r_{1} and r2r_{2}. The proof of Theorem 3 then follows from checking that whenever π1​(Sr′3​(K))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r^{\prime}}(K)) is left-orderable, we can define a left-ordering of π1​(K)\pi_{1}(K) that restricts to yield a line of slope r′r^{\prime} in the peripheral subgroup (compare [6, Proof of Theorem 9]).

2. The proof of Theorem 4

We recall the construction of a cabled knot in order to fix notation. Consider the (p,q)(p,q)-torus knot Tp,qT_{p,q}, where p,q>0p,q>0 are relatively prime. As the closure of a pp-strand braid, this knot may be naturally viewed in a solid torus TT by removing a tubular neighbourhood of the braid axis. The complement of Tp,qT_{p,q} in TT is referred to as a (p,q)(p,q)-cable space. Now given any knot KK in S3S^{3}, the cable knot Cp,q​(K)C_{p,q}(K) is obtained by identifying the boundary of TT with the boundary of S3∖ν⁡(K)S^{3}\smallsetminus\nu(K), identifying the longitude of TT with the longitude λ\lambda of KK. We will denote this cable knot by CC whenever this simplified notation does not cause confusion.

The knot group π1​(C)\pi_{1}(C) may be calculate via the Seifert-Van Kampen Theorem, by viewing the complement S3∖ν⁡(C)S^{3}\smallsetminus\nu(C) as the identification of the boundaries of S3∖ν⁡(K)S^{3}\smallsetminus\nu(K) and a solid torus D2×S1D^{2}\times S^{1} along an essential annulus with core curve given by the slope μq​λp\mu^{q}\lambda^{p}. If π1​(D2×S1)=⟨t⟩\pi_{1}(D^{2}\times S^{1})=\langle t\rangle then this gives rise to a natural amalgamated product

π1​(C)≅π1​(K)∗μq​λp=tpℤ.\pi_{1}(C)\cong\pi_{1}(K)\ast_{\mu^{q}\lambda^{p}=t^{p}}\mathbb{Z}.

Consulting [6, Section 3], the meridian and longitude for CC may be calculated as

μC=μu​λv​t−vandλC=μC−p​q​tp\mu_{C}=\mu^{u}\lambda^{v}t^{-v}\quad{\rm and}\quad\lambda_{C}=\mu_{C}^{-pq}t^{p}

where uu and vv are positive integers satisfying p​u−q​v=1pu-qv=1 (compare [20, Proof of Theorem 3.1]).

Suppose that the knot KK is rr-decayed, and choose cabling coefficients pp and qq so that q/p>rq/p>r. To begin, we choose a positive cone 𝒫⊂π1​(C)\mathcal{P}\subset\pi_{1}(C) and assume that μCp​q​λ=tp\mu_{C}^{pq}\lambda=t^{p} is positive. This means that tp=μq​λp∈𝒫t^{p}=\mu^{q}\lambda^{p}\in\mathcal{P}, so every element μm​λn\mu^{m}\lambda^{n} is positive whenever m/n>rm/n>r, since KK is rr-decayed.

Our method of proof will be to check that the cable is p​qpq-decayed by using the equivalence from Proposition 9. In particular, we will show that for the given positive cone 𝒫⊂π1​(C)\mathcal{P}\subset\pi_{1}(C) there exists an unbounded sequence of increasing rationals {ri}\{r_{i}\} with r0=p​qr_{0}=pq, such that our assumption αp​q=μCp​q​λC∈𝒫\alpha_{pq}=\mu_{C}^{pq}\lambda_{C}\in\mathcal{P} implies αri∈𝒫\alpha_{r_{i}}\in\mathcal{P} for all i>0i>0.

First consider the case when μC\mu_{C} is positive in the left-ordering defined by 𝒫\mathcal{P}. Here, μCp​q+N​λC\mu_{C}^{pq+N}\lambda_{C} is positive for N≥0N\geq 0, as it is a product of positive elements. Therefore in this case it suffices to choose ri=p​q+ir_{i}=pq+i for all i≥0i\geq 0.

For the remainder of the proof, we assume that μC\mu_{C} is negative. For repeated use below, we also observe the crucial identity

(t−v)p​(μu​λv)p=(tp)−v​μu​p​λv​p=μ−q​v​λ−p​v​μu​p​λv​p=μp​v−q​u=μ,(t^{-v})^{p}(\mu^{u}\lambda^{v})^{p}=(t^{p})^{-v}\mu^{up}\lambda^{vp}=\mu^{-qv}\lambda^{-pv}\mu^{up}\lambda^{vp}=\mu^{pv-qu}=\mu,

and recall that tpt^{p} commutes with μ,λ,μC\mu,\lambda,\mu_{C}, and λC\lambda_{C}. Therefore, we also have

(μu​λv)p​(t−v)p=(t−v)p​(μu​λv)p=μ.(\mu^{u}\lambda^{v})^{p}(t^{-v})^{p}=(t^{-v})^{p}(\mu^{u}\lambda^{v})^{p}=\mu.

Let kk be an arbitrary non-negative integer, and consider the element

3. Surgery on satellites

Let TT denote the solid torus containing a knot KPK^{P}, we require that KPK^{P} is not contained in any 33-ball inside TT. The knot KPK^{P} will be called the pattern knot. Let KCK^{C} denote a knot in S3S^{3}, KCK^{C} will be called the companion knot. We construct the satellite knot KK with pattern KPK^{P} and companion KCK^{C} as follows.

Let h:∂T→∂(S3∖ν⁡(KC))h:\partial T\rightarrow\partial(S^{3}\smallsetminus\nu(K^{C})) denote a diffeomorphism from the boundary of TT to the boundary of the complement of ν⁡(KC)\nu(K^{C}), which carries the longitude of ∂T\partial T onto the longitude of the knot KCK^{C}. The knot KK is then realized as the image of the knot KPK^{P} in the manifold

S3∖ν(KC)⊔hT=S3.S^{3}\smallsetminus\nu(K^{C})\sqcup_{h}T=S^{3}.
Lemma 15.

[19, Proposition 3.4] There exists a homomorphism ϕ:π1​(K)→π1​(KP)\phi:\pi_{1}(K)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(K^{P}) that perserves peripheral structure.

Proof.

We can compute the fundamental group π1​(K)\pi_{1}(K) by using the Seifert-Van Kampen theorem. Since

S3∖ν(K)=S3∖ν(KC)⊔hT∖ν(KP),S^{3}\smallsetminus\nu(K)=S^{3}\smallsetminus\nu(K^{C})\sqcup_{h}T\smallsetminus\nu(K^{P}),

the group π1​(K)\pi_{1}(K) is the free product π1​(KC)∗π1​(T∖ν⁡(KP))\pi_{1}(K^{C})*\pi_{1}(T\smallsetminus\nu(K^{P})), with amalgamation as follows: The meridian of KCK^{C} is identified with the meridian of TT, and the longitude of KCK^{C} is identified with the longitude of TT.

Let NN denote the normal closure in π1​(K)\pi_{1}(K) of the commutator subgroup of π1​(KC)\pi_{1}(K^{C}). The quotient π1​(K)/N\pi_{1}(K)/N can be considered as the result of killing the longitude of TT. Topologically we can think of this quotient as gluing a second solid torus T′T^{\prime} to the torus TT containing KPK^{P}, in such a way that the meridian of T′T^{\prime} is glued to the longitude of TT. The result is that π1​(KC)\pi_{1}(K^{C}) collapses to a single infinite cyclic subgroup, and the group π1​(K)/N\pi_{1}(K)/N is isomorphic to π1​(KP)\pi_{1}(K^{P}). The desired homomorphism ϕ\phi is the quotient map π1​(K)→π1​(K)/N\pi_{1}(K)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(K)/N. ∎

Proposition 16.

Suppose that KK is a satellite knot with pattern knot KPK^{P}, and r∈ℚr\in\mathbb{Q} is any rational number. If π1​(Sr3​(KP))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(K^{P})) is left-orderable and Sr3​(K)S^{3}_{r}(K) is irreducible, then π1​(Sr3​(K))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(K)) is left-orderable.

Proof.

By Lemma 15, there exists a homomorphism ϕ:π1​(K)→π1​(KP)\phi\colon\thinspace\pi_{1}(K)\rightarrow\pi_{1}(K^{P}) that preserves peripheral structure, so there exists an induced map

ϕr:π1​(Sr3​(K))→π1​(Sr3​(KP))\phi_{r}:\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(K))\rightarrow\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(K^{P}))

for every r∈ℚr\in\mathbb{Q}. Whenever π1​(Sr3​(KP))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(K^{P})) is left-orderable the image of ϕr\phi_{r} is nontrivial and π1​(Sr3​(K))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(K)) is left-orderable [2, Theorem 1.1] . ∎

Proof of Theorem 6.

By [7], p​qpq-surgery on a (p,q)(p,q)-cable knot yields a reducible manifold. Since the minimal geometric intersection number between reducible slopes is ±1\pm 1 [8], rr-surgery on a (p,q)(p,q)-cable yields an irreducible manifold whenever r<p​q−p−qr<pq-p-q. Moreover, a (p,q)(p,q)-cable knot can be described as a satellite knot with pattern knot Tp,qT_{p,q}, the (p,q)(p,q)-torus knot. Therefore, for r<p​q−p−qr<pq-p-q we can apply Proposition 16 to conclude that π1​(Sr3​(K))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(K)) will be left-orderable whenever π1​(Sr3​(Tp,q))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(T_{p,q})) is left-orderable.

We may now combine known results for surgery on torus knots in this setting. On the one hand, π1​(Sr3​(Tp,q))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(T_{p,q})) is an L-space whenever r≥2​g−1r\geq 2g-1 [14, Proposition 9.5] (see in particular [9, Lemma 2.13]), where g=g⁡(Tp,q)g=g(T_{p,q}) is the Seifert genus given by g⁡(Tp,q)=12​(p−1)​(q−1)g(T_{p,q})=\frac{1}{2}(p-1)(q-1). On the other, since Sr3​(Tp,q)S^{3}_{r}(T_{p,q}) is Seifert fibred or a connect sum of lens spaces for every rr [13], Sr3​(Tp,q)S^{3}_{r}(T_{p,q}) is an L-space if and only if π1​(Sr3​(Tp,q))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(T_{p,q})) is not left-orderable [1] (see also [16, 21]). In particular, π1​(Sr3​(Tp,q))\pi_{1}(S^{3}_{r}(T_{p,q})) is left-orderable whenever rr is less than 2​g​(Tp,q)−12g(T_{p,q})-1 and the result follows. ∎
